title: TB6-17283
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Appellant appeals the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision of November 2, 2016, that he is not a Convention Refugee.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of China. The Appellant appeals the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision of November 2, 2016, that he is not a Convention Refugee. The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that there is not more than a mere possibility that the Appellant would be persecuted for a Convention ground or that it is likely he would be subjected personally to a risk to his life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture.

The Appellant respectfully requests that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and find that he is a Convention refugee. Alternatively, he submits that the claim should be referred back to the RPD for re-determination.
Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD. Memorandum of Appeal

The Appeal gives rise to the following issues: a. Did the Panel err in finding that the Appellant could not have exited China on his own genuine passport even with the help of the smuggler? b. Did the Panel err in finding that the Appellant was not wanted by the Public Security Bureau because of the Appellant's political activities? c. Did the Panel err in assessing the Appellant's corroborative documentation and specifically, the Appellant's summons? d. Did the Panel err in its assessment of the Appellant's religious affiliation? Background

The Appellant described his family situation and the medical difficulties with their son. When the medical difficulties were not solved by doctors, the Appellant's wife started practicing Roman Catholicism. As a result of the Appellant's wife's practice, their son's condition gradually got better.

The Appellant declined his wife's offer of joining the church, but he did volunteer work when he had time. The Appellant's wife's church received an expropriation letter early in June 2016. The church members did not agree, stating that the building was located beside an area of expropriation. On June 16, 2016, government officers came with bulldozers and construction workers to try and demolish the building. The Appellant confronted the workers, yelling at them, and stating that Chinese citizens had no rights.

After the workers began beating the citizens, the Appellant escaped and went into hiding. He was informed that the police had come and accused him of being involved in illegal religious activities, and having interfered with the work of the government by taking the lead in protesting against the government. After failing to report, the Public Security Bureau (PSB) returned to his home and his relative's homes looking for him. As a result, the Appellant enlisted the support of a smuggler to improperly obtain a Canadian visa, and he left China on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX

After arriving in Canada, the Appellant learned that the church building had been torn down. The PSB continued to look for him, and a summons was issued ordering him to report to the PSB. The Appellant fears that if he returned to China he would be arrested and jailed.
The RPD hearing was held on October 21, 2016, and in a decision of November 2, 2016, the RPD found that the Appellant was neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The RPD decision was appealed to the Refugee Appeal Divison (RAD). In a decision of March 23, 2017, the RAD upheld the RPD decision and found that the Appellant was neither a Convention refugee nor person in need of protection.

The RAD decision was appealed to the Federal Court and in a decision on November 24, 2017, the Hon. Mr. Justice Campbell set aside the RAD decision and sent the matter back for re-determination by a different RAD member.

The Appellant was supportive of the standard of review outlined in the decision of the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) in Huruglica.1 This decision provides guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal, such as the RAD, to decisions of the first-level administrative tribunal.

The FCA stated that, with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law), which raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions by applying the correctness standard. Pursuant to paragraph 111(2)(b) of the IRPA, the RAD may refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination if it is "of the opinion" that it cannot make a decision confirming or setting aside the RPD's decision without hearing the evidence presented before the RPD. For questions of fact, mixed fact and law, and law, I have applied the standard of correctness, as per Huruglica. In assessing issues involving credibility of oral testimony, I have applied the RAD modified standard of reasonableness in those situations where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in making a particular finding, as per the decision in X (Re), 2017 CanLII 33034 (CA IRB). It further indicates that, although the RAD should sometimes exercise a degree of restraint before substituting its own determination, the issue of whether the circumstances warrant such restraint ought to be addressed on a case-by-case basis.
Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its assessment of the RPD's decision on the basis of the principles outlined above. MERITS OF THE APPEAL Credibility The Summons

The RPD doubted the veracity of the summons2 submitted in documentation because of credibility findings and his ability to leave China using his own travel documents. The RPD noted that the summons was a single page with black ink and red stamps, without any security features, and could easily be made by anyone anywhere. The RPD quoted documentation regarding fraudulent documentation in China.3

Quoting Federal jurisprudence,4 the Appellant submits that the Panel erred by applying "reverse reasoning" to analyze the Appellant's summons. He stated that it is impermissible for the member to first commit herself to the conclusion that he is not wanted because he was able to exit China on his own genuine passport when allegedly being wanted by the PSB, and then negate the Appellant summons that he is indeed wanted by the PSB. The Appellant also quoted Ren v Canada, 2015 FC 1402 to support his submissions.

The Appellant further submits that there was nothing on the face of the summons to suggest it was not authentic and that the Board was required to squarely address the document and not just dismiss it as a result of prior credibility findings. The Appellant also submitted that he presented falsified documents to travel to Canada and that the smuggler filled out the application. The Appellant further submitted that when fleeing the country, fraudulent documents must sometimes be used in order to guarantee the person being persecuted safe passage and should not be used to impugn the credibility of the Appellant.5 Given the above, the Appellant submits that the summons should not be assigned no weight.

Although there is Federal jurisprudence to support transferring credibility issues to other aspects of the claim, the RAD is an agreement with the Appellant that the RPD's findings were insufficient to completely negate the summons. There is also Federal jurisprudence to support that the seal could be considered as a security feature. However, the RAD finds that the Public Security Bureau summons, referenced above and submitted in documentation, is fraudulent and draws a negative credibility inference.

A government issued summons (zhi'an chuanhuan) was submitted to verify that Appellant was wanted by the Chinese authorities. In observing the NDP documentation,6 the RAD notes the following: "there has been no variation in the format of summonses and subpoenas since 2003 (ibid. 22 June 2013)." The documentation goes on to quote that such forms are supposed to be used throughout the country and that "regional variations are not meant to exist." Observing the summons submitted in documentation and comparing it to the samples in the NDP documentation,7 the RAD finds that structure and format of the summons is not consistent with the documentation.

The identifier of the individual named and located on the top left of the sample NDP summons, is missing. The structure of the second and third line are inconsistent with the NDP documentation, specifically the Chinese character before the number 30 is on the second line not the third. In observing the spacing for the bottom three lines of the document, the RAD finds that it is inconsistent with the documentation, provided in the NDP, in both location on the document and character sizing.

In observing the Chinese characters where the Seal of the Public Security Authority is placed, the RAD finds that they are inconsistent with the documentation. The NDP documentation has 6 Chinese characters enclosed by parenthesis while the document presented has 5. At the bottom of the document where the information for the alleged perpetrator is given, there is a Chinese character on the third line to indicate where the perpetrator is to sign. That character is missing on the summons submitted in documentation.

The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the summons submitted is fraudulent, and draws a negative inference regarding the Appellant's credibility in submitting a fraudulent document to support his case.

Given this fraudulent documentation, the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant was not wanted by the PSB or the authorities in China as alleged. Given that there is no credible documentation given to support his allegations of being wanted by the authorities, the RAD finds the Appellant is not a credible witness about his allegations and finds that a determinative basis of his claim, i.e. being wanted by the authorities in China for his alleged political activities against the government, is not credible. Given this finding, the RAD finds that the Appellant could have left China on his own documentation without difficulty, and that the allegations that he used a smuggler to arrange his exit from China, are not credible. The fact that the Appellant used fraudulent information on his Canadian visa application is not a determinative issue in this claim. Exit from China

The RPD found that the Appellant was not wanted by the Chinese authorities because he was able to exit China using his own documentation. The RPD explained at length the efficacy of Chinese authorities in apprehending Chinese citizens when they attempt to leave China.8 The panel noted there was systematic corruption in China and that airport officials can be bribed and that documentary evidence indicates the authorities in China do not always apply regulations evenly. However, the RPD found that the preponderance of documentary evidence states that authorities at airports and borders conduct a thorough screening of passengers. In that the Appellant testified that he is wanted for arrest, the RPD preferred the unbiased country conditions evidence to his testimony. The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant was not wanted by the Chinese authorities having exited on his own identity documents.

The Appellant submits that the RPD erred when it found that he could not have exited China on his own passport if he was wanted by the PSB. The Appellant further submits that the RPD erred by preferring one type of evidence over another. The Appellant submitted Federal jurisprudence to support its submission that a person could be wanted by the authorities and be able to bypass border security using their own passport.9 The Appellant further references NDP documentation regarding the "endemic" fraud and bribery among enforcers of the law.
The Appellant further submits that the RPD erred by not asking the Appellant about the support given to him by the smuggler when he went through customs.

Above in this decision, the RAD found that the documentation submitted, to support that the Appellant was wanted by the Chinese authorities, was fraudulent. The documentation and testimony of the Appellant that he was able to leave China without difficulty supports the RAD's finding above. Given that there is no probative documentation that he was wanted by the authorities, the Appellant could have left China without difficulty providing he had the appropriate documentation. The RAD also finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant did not use a smuggler as alleged. Political Activities

The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony about his behaviour at the alleged protest to be implausible and unlikely. The RPD reasoned that the Appellant was not a member of the church, did not own the land being expropriated, and that he ran away before the PSB officers arrived. The RPD did not accept his explanation when the testified that the PSB could get information about him as a reason for running away. The RPD further reasoned that the Appellant's wife was a member of the church, participated in the protest, was not arrested, and according to testimony she remains in the family home and continues to be employed.

When questioned on his alleged leadership, the RPD found that he did not explain in any way how he was a leader as he did not plan the protest, did not write anything to the government, and his name does not appear in any related documentation. In that the Appellant did not have a history of protesting anything, the RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that if he was perceived to be an irritant or threat to the government, he would not have been permitted to leave China.

The Appellant submits that even though he was not a member of the church congregation, he was deeply involved because of his involvement as a volunteer. The Appellant further submits that his BOC narrative10 outlines his involvement in the protest. He further submits that the RPD did not ask questions or express concerns regarding this aspect of the evidence. He further submits that the RPD ignored relevant evidence and failed to consider the plausibility and ease with which the PSB could identify the Appellant and therefore require his arrest.

Above in this decision, the RAD found that the Appellant was not wanted by the PSB as alleged. This fact undermines the Appellant's documentation and testimony that he was involved in a protest as a leader and went into hiding. The RAD has reviewed the testimony of the Appellant regarding his alleged leadership, and finds, on a balance of probabilities, that his testimony was not probative in confirming this allegation. The allegations in the Appellant's BOC narrative have not been substantiated.

If in fact the protest was held, as testimony and documentation attest to, the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the ensuing allegations of hiding and potential arrest are not credible. Documentation

In reviewing the documentation11 concerning the land expropriation, the RPD finds that the Appellant's name is not on any of these documents nor do they substantiate his assertion that he participated in a demonstration and clashed with workers there.
The Appellant, as outlined above, focused his submissions on the genuineness of the summons. That issue has been addressed above.

In reviewing the land expropriation document submitted, the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant's name does not appear, nor does it provide any probative information about his allegations of a protest and potential incarceration by the authorities. Religious Affiliation

The RPD noted that the Appellant testified that he was not a member of the church congregation in China but that he now attends a church in Canada and provided a letter12 from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXto support this allegation. The RPD noted that the Appellant testified that he chose this church for the convenience of where he lived, was not yet baptized, and found, on a balance of probabilities, that he was not yet a practicing Catholic.

The RPD quoted NDP documentation to support that the Catholic Church is recognized by Chinese authorities and that they generally tolerate small house church groups. Further the documentation indicates that millions of Chinese live and worship in China.13 The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that should he wish to worship on his return to China, there are many congregations he could attend without attracting the interest of authorities.

The Appellant submits that he provided sufficient evidence to establish his religious identity and that he regularly participates in church activities, has knowledge of Christianity, and has pictures of himself at church practicing his religion. He submits that the RPD erred by doubting the genuineness of his practice because of his testimony regarding the geographical proximity of the church he attends.

Referencing Federal jurisprudence,14 the Appellant submits that the RPD erred when it stated that the Appellant could choose any number of churches upon his return to China. The NDP documentation15 indicates that the Pope is not recognized by the Patriotic church in China and this nonrecognition constitutes significant doctrinal differences. He submits that serious restrictions are not limited to arrest and detention but restrictions in the ability to practice in public, preach, and had the benefits of religious instruction and leadership.

The RAD has reviewed all of the documentation in this case and finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant could return to China without fear of persecution. His wife, according to documentation and testimony, practices Roman Catholicism in China without any persecution or fear from the Chinese authorities. The Appellant has begun his religious practice in Canada and although he was not yet baptized or officially a member of the Roman Catholic Church at the time of the RPD hearing, he has indicated, according to the letter submitted, an interest in pursuing this religion. The RAD notes that this letter was dated October 20, 2016, 16and states that he was to have successfully completed the program as of July 8, 2017, Parish Day. No additional documentation was submitted on appeal to confirm that the Appellant has continued this practice of Roman Catholicism or has been baptized.

The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant could return to China without fear of persecution and continue, with his wife, if he so desires, the practice of his newfound religion. Disposition

The RAD confirms the RPD's determination and dismisses the appeal according to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA. The RAD finds that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee, nor person in need of protection. (signed) "Robert S. Garner" Robert S. Garner November 1, 2018 Date 1 M.C.I. v.
